sentences.text: He built a chess robot that could beat anyone, and before every game, he opened it up to prove it was empty.
You see, it's 1770, and an inventor has just rolled a wooden cabinet into the Empress's palace in Vienna.
On top sits a life-size wooden man in a turban, staring at a chessboard.
The whole court laughs.
So he opens the doors one by one and holds a candle behind them.
Nothing but gears.
He winds a key, the gears tick, and the Turk lifts its arm.
The first count brave enough to play it loses.
Nobody's laughing now.
For eighty years the Turk tours the world.
It beats Benjamin Franklin.
And when Napoleon tries to cheat, it puts his piece back.
Twice.
The third time, it sweeps every piece off the board.
Then in 1854, a fire burns the Turk to ash, and its secret finally comes out.
There was a man inside.
A chess master, folded into the cabinet.
When each door opened, he slid his seat to the other side, behind fake gears.
Magnets under the board showed him every move, and a lever moved the Turk's hand.
The robot that beat Napoleon was a man in a box, playing by candlelight.
